stemMd: According to Raut, the single-activity rule was especially likely to hide care that:

options.label: A
options.textMd: filled an entire ten- or fifteen-minute diary interval by itself.

options.label: B
options.textMd: consisted of staying available while some other, nameable task was under way.

options.label: C
options.textMd: was carried out by paid workers rather than by family members.

options.label: D
options.textMd: took place outside the respondent's own household.

explanationMd:
The third paragraph gives both the claim and the reason. Raut's claim is that the rule "systematically undercounted the kind of care that consists of being available — supervision, vigilance, the readiness to intervene." Her reason is the clause that follows: "precisely because such care rarely displaces another task."

Put the two together. If a kind of care never takes over the whole interval, it is always competing with something else for the single slot, and it always loses to the activity with a name — which is why the parent "folding laundry while supervising a toddler recorded laundry." Choice B states exactly that condition.

Check the answer by running the rule in reverse. Which care would the single-activity rule capture perfectly? Care that occupies an interval on its own, with nothing to compete against. That is choice A, which is the opposite of what the passage says is hidden — a useful sign that B is right.

distractorRationale.d: Introduces a distinction by location that the passage never makes. The examples given — meals cooked, children supervised, elderly relatives visited — are not sorted by where they happen, and the coding rule operates on time intervals, not places.
distractorRationale.c: Reverses the passage's concern. Paragraph 1 says unpaid work was the work that went unrecorded "because none of it was paid"; paid care has an occupation and a job title and is precisely the kind of work the older surveys could already see.
distractorRationale.a: Names the case the single-activity rule handles correctly. Care that fills an interval by itself has no competing activity to be displaced by, so it is recorded; the passage says the hidden care is the sort that "rarely displaces another task."

accessibilityText: The question asks which kind of care the sociologist Raut says was systematically undercounted by a coding rule that allowed only one activity to be recorded in each diary interval.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original passage. Not derived from, and not a paraphrase of, any ACT-published question.

review.author: enhanced-act-topup-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Raut says the rule undercounted care that consists of being available (supervision, vigilance), because such care rarely displaces another task, which is (b). (a) describes care that would be recorded as the primary activity. (c) and (d) are not raised; the passage concerns unpaid care, and location is never discussed.

review.notes: Author solved the item and tried to defend each distractor. A adds a location criterion absent from the passage, B inverts the paid/unpaid distinction of paragraph 1, C describes the case the rule records correctly rather than the case it hides.
